title: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica
wiki_lead:
Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (English: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), often called simply the Principia (), is a book by Sir Isaac Newton that expounds Newton's laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation.
The Principia is written in Latin and comprises three volumes, and was authorized (imprimatur) by Samuel Pepys, then-president of the Royal Society on 5 July 1686 and first published in 1687. After annotating and correcting his personal copy of the first edition, Newton published two further editions, one of 1713 with errors in the 1687 version corrected, and another, improved one of 1726.
The Principia forms a mathematical foundation for the theory of classical mechanics, and is generally considered to be one of the most important works in the history of science. It has been referred to as "the greatest scientific work in history" and "the supreme expression in human thought of the mind's ability to hold the universe fixed as an object of contemplation".
Recent research has challenged the long-held view that the Principia had only a limited initial readership, suggesting that its early influence on Enlightenment science was substantially greater than previously recognized. 
In formulating his physical laws, Newton developed and used mathematical methods now included in the field of calculus, expressing them in the form of geometric propositions about "vanishingly small" shapes. In a revised conclusion to the Principia (see § General Scholium), Newton emphasized the empirical nature of the work with the expression Hypotheses non fingo ("I frame/feign no hypotheses"). Among other achievements, Newton provides an explanation for Johannes Kepler's laws of planetary motion, which Kepler had obtained empirically. Newton also set out four rules of scientific reasoning that helped shape modern approaches to science.
grok_lead: PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Latin for Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), often referred to simply as the Principia, is a seminal work in three books written by the English mathematician, physicist, and astronomer Sir Isaac Newton. First published in 1687 under the auspices of the Royal Society, it establishes the foundational principles of classical mechanics through rigorous mathematical demonstrations. The book articulates Newton's three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, providing a unified framework that explains both terrestrial and celestial phenomena. The Principia is structured into three books, each building upon the previous to develop Newton's system of the world. Book I introduces the method of first principles, including definitions of key concepts like absolute space and time, followed by the laws of motion and their applications to centripetal forces and orbital mechanics. Book II examines motion in resisting media, such as fluids, to refute alternative theories like Descartes' vortices. Book III, titled "The System of the World," applies these principles to astronomical observations, deriving the inverse-square law of gravitation and explaining planetary motions, tides, and comets. Written in Latin, the original text employs geometric proofs rather than the calculus Newton had developed, reflecting his intent to make the work accessible to contemporary scholars. Subsequent editions refined the Principia 's content: the second edition in 1713 included an editorial preface by Roger Cotes and addressed philosophical critiques, while the third edition in 1726 incorporated updated astronomical data and further clarifications shortly before Newton's death in 1727. Prompted by Edmond Halley's inquiries into orbital mechanics, the work emerged from Newton's private studies amid the scientific revolution, synthesizing ideas from Copernicus, Galileo, and Kepler into a mathematically precise system. The Principia revolutionized science by demonstrating that the same physical laws govern the heavens and Earth, laying the groundwork for modern physics, astronomy, and engineering. Its influence persists, serving as a cornerstone for Newtonian mechanics until the advent of relativity and quantum theory in the 20th century, and it remains one of the most cited works in the history of science.
